notes.text: Wisdom — Having expressed the counsels of wicked men, he now declares the voice of wisdom. By wisdom he understands the wisdom of God revealed to men in his word. And this is said to cry with a loud voice, to intimate God's earnestness in inviting sinners to repentance. Abroad - Or, in the streets or open places. Not in corners, but openly before all the world.
Gates — Where magistrates sit in judgment, and people are assembled. The city - Not only in the gate, but in every part of the city.
Scoffers — That scoff at religion and contemn the word and faithful ministers of God.
My words — By my spirit I will cause you to understand my word.
Called — By my ministers, by my judgments, and by the motions of my spirit and your own conscience.
Your fear — The misery you do or should fear.
Early — With diligence and fervency.
Knowledge — The practical knowledge of God and of their duty.
Eat — They should receive punishment answerable to their sins. Filled - With the fruits of them.

Turning — From God. Destroy - Shall prove the occasion of their ruin, by making them presumptuous, and secure. Solomon shews, that they who diligently seek wisdom shall find it, ver. 1-9. He shews the advantage of it, that it would preserve them from evil men, ver. 10-15. And evil women, ver. 16-19. And would lead them into, and keep them in the way of good men, ver. 20-22.

glossa.text:
*Wisdom.* Thus far the persecutions which the Jews brought upon Christ; from here, those things which he speaks through the apostles to those same persecutors after the passion. *Wisdom,* that is Christ, speaks *abroad,* that is, openly in the light, that, infancy being left behind, they may be little ones in malice.

 ((RAB.)) For Christ is indeed the Wisdom of God, etc., *as far as* they should say to anyone.

*Abroad.* ((ID.)) Openly, after the resurrection, etc., *as far as: in the street his voice.*

*In the streets she uttereth her voice,* etc. The things which he had taught before few he plainly repeated, whence: *The things which I say to you in the darkness, speak ye into the light.*

*At the head of the crowds she crieth out,* etc. ((ID.)) Because even to the princes, who seemed to have prevailed against him so that he should be crucified, he openly recalled to memory the guilt of the murder which they had perpetrated, and called them to the remedy of penance.

*In the doors of the gates of the city.* ((ID.)) The city of the Lord, the Church gathered into one out of both peoples, etc., *as far as* he called back his own grace; so that, as Luke says: *A great multitude of the priests should obey the faith ((Act. VI))*.

*How long. Now* you have seen Christ in the flesh working miracles, whom you have despised: now at least love him raised up from death, and he will forgive what you have sinned.

*Little ones.* ((RAB.)) Those slower in understanding are called little ones, etc., *as far as* which the Son himself, coming, conferred upon those perfect in understanding?

*Be ye converted.* Wisdom exhorts them to be converted to God, and puts forth the spirit.

*To correction.* Through the apostles he rebukes the Jews, and admonishes them to be converted at least after the ascension and the resurrection.
*I also.* ((ID.)) Likewise in the psalm, etc., *as far as* as though they despised nothing.

*When sudden calamity shall rush in.* He speaks of the sudden siege of Jerusalem and the storming of the whole province wrought by the Romans. Of which, *Seeing the city, he wept over it ((Luc. XIX))*.

*When it shall come upon you.* ((RAB.)) This whole correction of wisdom can, etc., *as far as* for that which follows,

*They shall rise early and shall not find me,* signifies the time of judgment, in which some shall rise again unto life, others unto everlasting reproach.

*They shall call upon me.* The Jews are not read to have called upon the Lord in the siege; and even if some did call upon him, because they did not truly repent, they were not heard.
*They have held it hateful.* The just man on the contrary, *The unjust,* he says, *have I hated, and thy law have I loved.*

*They shall eat therefore.* ((ID.)) Because they would not walk in my ways, etc., *as far as and it shall be well with thee.*

*And they shall be filled with their own devices.* By which they were saying, etc., *as far as* it can be taken.

*Turning away.* Turning away and prosperity destroys, when the mind turned away from the fear of its Maker seems, by the anger of that same Maker, to suffer nothing adverse in those things wherein it sins. But as Job says: *They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they go down to hell.*

*Of little ones.* In understanding, whence above, etc., *as far as* but because they turn away, they kill themselves.
*But he that shall hear me, without terror shall rest,* etc. It can be understood in this life, and in the life to come, etc., *as far as* of the resurrection he shall rest.

notes.text: The heavens — They are as a legible book, wherein he that runs may read it. The glory - His eternal power and Godhead, his infinite wisdom and goodness. Firmament - Or, the expansion, all the vast space extended from the earth to the highest heavens, with all its goodly furniture.

Day — Every day and night repeats these demonstrations of God's glory. Uttereth - Or, poureth forth, constantly and abundantly, as a fountain doth water; So this Hebrew word signifies. Knowledge - Gives us a clear knowledge or discovery of God their author.

Heard — Or, understood; there are divers nations in the world, which have several languages, so that one cannot discourse with, or be understood by another, but the heavens are such an universal teacher, that they can speak to all people, and be clearly understood by all.

Line — Their lines, the singular number being put for the plural. And this expression is very proper, because the heavens do not teach men audibly, or by speaking to their ears, but visibly by propounding things to their eyes, which is done in lines or writings. Gone - Is spread abroad. Earth - So as to be seen and read, by all the inhabitants of the earth. Words - Their magnificent structure, their exquisite order, and most regular course, by which they declare their author, no less than men discover their minds by their words. Sun - Which being the most illustrious and useful of all the heavenly bodies, is here particularly mentioned.

Bridegroom — Gloriously adorned with light as with a beautiful garment, and smiling upon the world with a pleasant countenance. Chamber - In which he is poetically supposed to have rested all night, and thence to break forth as it were on a sudden. Strong man - Conscious and confident of his own strength.
The ends — His course is constant from east to west, and thence to the east again. So that there is no part of the earth which doth not one time or other feel the benefit of his light and heat.

The law — The doctrine delivered to his church, whether by Moses, or by other prophets. Having discoursed hitherto of the glory of God shining forth in, the visible heavens, he now proceeds to another demonstration of God's glory, which he compares with and prefers before the former. Perfect - Completely discovering both the nature and will of God, and the whole duty of man, what he is to believe and practice, and whatsoever is necessary to his present and eternal happiness. Whereas the creation, although it did declare so much of God, as left all men without excuse, yet did not fully manifest the will of God, nor bring men to eternal salvation. Converting - From sin to God, from whom all men are naturally revolted. Testimony - His law, so called because it is a witness between God and man, what God requires of man, and what upon the performance of that condition, he will do for man. Sure - Hebrew. faithful or true, which is most necessary in a witness: it will not mislead any man, but will infallibly bring him to happiness. Simple - Even persons of the lowest capacities.

Right — Both in themselves, and in their effect, as guiding men in the ready way to eternal happiness. Rejoicing - By the discoveries of God's love to sinful men, in offers and promises of mercy. Commandment - All his commands. Pure - Without the least mixture of error. The eyes - Of the mind, with a compleat manifestation of God's will and man's duty: both which, the works of nature, and all the writings of men discover but darkly and imperfectly.

The fear — The law and word of God, because it is both the object and the rule, and the cause of holy fear. Clean - Sincere, not adulterated with any mixture. Constant and unchangeable, the same for substance in all ages. Judgments - God's laws are frequently called his judgments, because they are the declarations of his righteous will, and as it were his judicial sentence by which he expects that men should govern themselves, and by which he will judge them at the last day.

Who — Thy law, O Lord, is holy and just and good. But I fall infinitely short of it. Cleanse - Both by justification, through the blood of thy son; and by sanctification thro' thy Holy Spirit. Though the first may seem to be principally intended, because he speaks of his past sins. Secret - From the guilt of such sins as were secret either, from others; such as none knows but God and my own conscience: or, from myself; such as I never observed, or did not discern the evil of. Pardon my unknown sins, of which I never repented particularly, as I should have done.

Presumptuous — From known and evident sins, such as are committed against knowledge, against the checks of conscience, and the motions of God's spirit. Dominion - If I be at any time tempted to such sins, Lord let them not prevail over me, and if I do fall into them, let me speedily rise again.

Let — Having prayed that God would keep him from sinful actions, he now prays that God would govern, and sanctify his words and thoughts: and this was necessary to preserve him from presumptuous sins, which have their first rise in the thoughts. Redeemer - This expression seems to be added emphatically, and with special respect to Christ, to whom alone this word Goel can properly belong. A prayer for the king, ver. 1-4. The king and the people rejoice in God, and pray for his help, ver. 5-9. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The heavens shew forth. ((Ibid.))* First, speaking of the incarnation, he commends the preaching of the new law. ((AUG.)) The heavens, the apostles, concerning the glory of Christ in which he is equal to the Father. ((CASS.)) Or the heavens, they who sent the star. *The glory. ((Ibid.))*: That God freely forgives sins. *The works.* ((AUG.)) Those which are according to man, etc., *as far as* and these same are made night to him, giving to the darkened the knowledge which is of things human. ((CASS.)) And this so wonderfully, that it is in all tongues; and so widely, that it is in every part of the compass of the earth.

*Day unto day.* ((CASS.)) He treats of it by demonstration. ((AUG.)) *Day unto day.* The Spirit brings forth to spiritual men the fullness of wisdom, etc., *as far as* this teaching is continued by days and by nights down to those who come after.

*Speeches.* ((CASS.)) Public persuadings. *Words.* Common narrations. *Whose voices are not heard.* He would say more plainly, in whom their voices are not heard, or, the voices of all their words are heard: he does the same thing by means of the relative.

((AUG.)) The Spirit made the first men speak with all tongues, he who was to gather all nations into one; then one man was for all, so now one Christ, head and body.

*In the sun* ((CASS.)) What he praises others for having done, he himself does: he preaches the incarnation. Or in the sun, in the open sight of the world, or in labour. The sun burns, and shines, and varies the seasons. *His tabernacle.* ((AUG.)) As it were a soldier's dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to storm the errors of the world. Or the tabernacle, the Church in the open, not in secret, so as to lie hid. *A bridegroom.* ((CASS.)) So often promised by the prophets, a great likeness of the sacrament: therefore born of a virgin, that he might join to himself the Church a virgin. *Out of his bride-chamber.* ((AUG.)) That is, the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Behold, humble in mercy, but strong in majesty. *As a giant to run.* ((CASS.)) Unshaken, not to be called back, overcoming human nature by his power. *From the highest.* Here the Trinity is shewn, etc., *as far as* it marks the unity of the Trinity. *Neither is there any that can hide himself,* etc. ((AUG.)) The Word made flesh permitted no man to excuse himself out of the shadow of death: because the heat of the Word pierced even that. Or, the heat is the Spirit, whom he sent when he had returned, who is law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear and judgments, because he does these things.

*The law of the Lord.* ((CAS.)) Secondly, he praises the precepts of the New and the Old Testament. ((Ibid.)) The law given through Moses, correcting all things by the distinction of its words, and sending them on to the grace of Christ. *Converting.* ((AUG.)) By liberty, unto the imitating of himself, not pressing down with the yoke of servitude. *Souls.* Wills, not merely hands, as the Old Testament did. *The testimony.* Whatsoever *Quaecunquae* testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and have given wisdom to the humble. *Wisdom:* concerning things divine.

*The justices of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* All are right in him, who taught not what he did not do, so that they who imitate them might rejoice in them, seeing they would do them freely with charity, not slavishly with fear. ((CASS.)) *Justices,* the law which justifies; whatsoever it commands is just.

*The fear of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not profitable, and it changes with the times. *The fear of the Lord* is without any perturbation, because it is a love mingled with dread, because if it fears the judge, it knows him merciful. ((AUG.)) Fear, not that penal fear for earthly things, for love of which the soul is afraid, but the chaste fear whereby, the more it loves, the more it is wary of offending the bridegroom, and therefore it is not cast out, but abides. *Judgments.* The judgments of God need not another's authority.

*Desirable things. ((Ibid.))* Or, much to be desired, or much gold and stone; or much that is precious. Desirable above gold, etc., *as far as,* whose will he sets before his own, and they are sweeter than he himself is to himself. *Above gold,* that is, everything that is sought after, whether for riches, or for power, or for pleasure. *Honey.* The food of God is honey; that is, one now loosed from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, because he is still wrapped about, for whom there is need of the pressure of God's hand squeezing him out, that he may go into life.

*Who understandeth sins. ((Ibid.))* Thirdly he asks to be purged of vices, that he may be a worthy psalmist, to report these sacraments. To a mind that sees, truth is sweet, and judgments sweet; to one that does not see, what sweetness is there? But why is it not seen? Because of sins: nor is it any wonder: *For who understandeth sins?* ((CASS.)) *Sins:* all of them, for certain of them are known. *Mine* defile, *others'* afflict, and now spare, drive back the persuader. *From my secret ones.* He includes all sins under two heads, etc., *as far as* whereby man was seduced; and by consenting he made it his own. ((AUG.)) There is no greater sin than to apostatize from God, which is the beginning of pride: but pride is the beginning and the cause of all sin.

notes.text: Be not many teachers — Let no more of you take this upon you than God thrusts out; seeing it is so hard not to offend in speaking much. Knowing that we - That all who thrust themselves into the office. Shall receive greater condemnation - For more offenses. St. James here, as in several of the following verses, by a common figure of speech, includes himself: we shall receive, - we offend, - we put bits, - we curse - None of which, as common sense shows, are to be interpreted either of him or of the other apostles.
The same is able to bridle the whole body — That is, the whole man. And doubtless some are able to do this, and so are in this sense perfect.
We — That is, men.
Boasteth great things — Hath great influence.

A world of iniquity — Containing an immense quantity of all manner of wickedness. It defileth - As fire by its smoke. The whole body - The whole man. And setteth on fire the course of nature - All the passions, every wheel of his soul.
Every kind — The expression perhaps is not to be taken strictly. Reptiles - That is, creeping things.
But no man can tame the tongue — Of another; no, nor his own, without peculiar help from God.
Men made after the likeness of God — Indeed we have now lost this likeness; yet there remains from thence an indelible nobleness, which we ought to reverence both in ourselves and others.

glossa.text:
*Be ye not many masters.* As I have admonished you to do works, so I admonish you to shun foolish masterships. *Be ye not many.* There were many in the times of the apostles who, coming down from Judaea to Antioch, not well instructed in the law of the faith, taught that believers from among the Gentiles ought to be circumcised, and brought in other errors, which brought upon the true preachers no small labour of controversy. These therefore he removes from the office of the word, lest they hinder the true preachers.

*Greater. ((BED.))* He who, being unlearned, usurps the office of teaching, and announces Christ not sincerely, deserves a greater damnation than if he alone should perish by his own wickedness; as, on the contrary, he who ministers well acquires for himself a good degree.

*In many things.* Truly it is perilous to wish to be set over the rest, because not only you who are less instructed, but we all preachers, even the greater, offend in many things, some by teaching ill, and others by living ill, and in other ways. The blessed Apostle numbers himself with them, that he may reprove the more freely. The just man offends in one way, the wicked in another; the just man by the frailty of the flesh, and he does not cease to be just, whence Solomon: *Seven times in the day shall the just man fall and shall rise again;* as the offence is daily, so daily is the remedy of prayers and of good works, but the wicked fall down into evil. *If any man.* He wishes to show the unavoidable offence of the word, that he may deter the unskilled, lest they desire preferment: because he who desires to be set over others must be more perfect than the rest, lest he offend when he ought to profit; but the unskilled are not able not to offend in preaching.

*Offendeth not in word. ((BED.))* In that word, namely, whose offence human frailty is able to avoid. As the word of guile, of detraction, of pride, of boasting, and also of idle and superfluous speech, *he is a perfect man.*

*But if we put bits into the mouths of horses. ((BED.))* Into our own mouths much more ought we to put them. Certain books have: *But as bits to horses,* and it is thus joined to what follows: *But as we put bits into the mouths of horses, so the tongue also is indeed a little member, and exalteth great things.*

*And exalteth great things. ((ID.))* Rewards, if the impulse of him that directs governs it well; if ill, it exalts great destruction for itself and for its own, whence Solomon: *Death and life are in the hands of the tongue ((Prov. XVIII))* . It exalts life, if it teaches the Church well; death, if ill. For the matter is against those who, destitute both of life and of knowledge, presumed to teach. Great things therefore does that tongue exalt which, despising the words and the meanings of others, singularly boasts itself wise *sapientiem* and eloquent. Against which: *Do not multiply to speak lofty things, glorying.*

*Behold how great a fire.* So too an incontinent tongue makes a great matter of good works to perish, and so, since it is almost impossible that the sin of the tongue be avoided even by the perfect, not everyone ought to seek the mastership.

*The universality of iniquity.* He says universality, because through it almost all crimes are either contrived, as robberies, ravishments: or are perpetrated, as perjuries, false testimonies: or are defended, as when any impure man, by excusing the wickedness he has committed, feigns the good which he has not done. *Which defileth the whole body.* And because the tongue is such, it defiles the whole body, and makes it be reckoned unclean in the sight of God, and therefore it is a grave thing to undergo the mastership: because *it is set among our members,* it is one of our members, exceedingly near to us.

*It inflameth the wheel,* etc. ((BED.)) It defiles the whole course of temporal life, etc., *as far as* it compels to bring it to effect through the other members.

*For every nature of beasts,* etc. ((ID.)) We read in Pliny that a most savage asp in Egypt was tamed by a certain householder, and, going forth daily from its cavern, was wont to receive its allowance from his table. We read in Marcellinus that a tigress, made tame, was sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.

*Out of the same mouth proceedeth.* Others, seeing what we do, are led on by our example, so that they likewise bless and curse. *It ought not.* Truly it ought not to be that with the same mouth we bless concerning the head and curse concerning the members, because by the bitterness of cursing the sweetness of blessing is consumed.

*Doth a fountain.* The preacher must sometimes use bitter preaching, by withdrawing, by rebuking. Which is difficult enough, that with different words tending to the same end he should be able to do both.

*Can, brethren.* It cannot come to pass that a teacher be a fig tree by the sweetness of the beatitude to which he exhorts, and use sweet words, and that he be a vine, making men forget all temporal things, for which it behoves to use harsh ones: this therefore is difficult. *So neither can the salt water make sweet water,* that is, a preacher sharply biting the manners of others cannot in the same teaching be sweet to those same men.

notes.text: Matt. xvi, 13; Luke ix, 18.

He enjoined them silence for the present,

1. That he might not encourage the people to set him up for a temporal king;

2. That he might not provoke the scribes and Pharisees to destroy him before the time and,

3. That he might not forestall the bright evidence which was to be given of his Divine character after his resurrection.

31. Matt. xvi, 21; Luke ix, 22.
He spake that saying openly — Or in express terms. Till now he had only intimated it to them. And Peter taking hold of him - Perhaps by the arms or clothes.
Looking on his disciples — That they might the more observe what he said to Peter.

And when he called the people — To hear a truth of the last importance, and one that equally concerned them all. Let him deny himself - His own will, in all things small and great, however pleasing, and that continually: And take up his cross - Embrace the will of God, however painful, daily, hourly, continually. Thus only can he follow me in holiness to glory.
Matt. xvi, 25; Luke ix, 24; Luke xvii, 33; John xii, 25.

Whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words — That is, avowing whatever I have said (particularly of self denial and the daily cross) both by word and action. Matt. x, 32; Luke ix, 26; Luke xii, 8.

glossa.text:
*Whom do men say that I am?* Fitly does he first ask the opinion of men, lest their confession should seem weakened by the opinion of the crowd, but by the acknowledging of the truth: lest, like Herod, they be thought to waver about the things they had heard. Whence he says to Peter, according to Matthew: *Flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee ((Matth. XVI))*, that is, the teaching of men.

*Men.* Fitly are they called men who after the manner of men bring forth a divergent opinion concerning the Lord. For they who with a pious mind acknowledge the truth of his power deserve to be called, not men, but gods. Whence he says to them: *But you,* etc. As if he said: They, being men, opine the things of men; but you, being gods, whom do you say that I am?

*Thou art the Christ. ((BEDA.))* He embraces all things who expresses both the nature and the name, in which is the sum of the virtues. Paul says, etc., *as far as* yet it is not permitted to be ignorant of the faith of his generation.

*And he charged them. ((BEDA.))* He would not have himself preached before the passion and the resurrection: because, the sacrament of his blood being accomplished, he says to the apostles more opportunely: *Going, teach ye all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost ((Matth. XVIII))*. Because it would not profit that he be publicly preached whom they were about to see scourged, and crucified, and suffering many things.

*That it behoveth,* etc. ((HIER.)) As a skilled pilot, guarding against a storm while it is calm, wills his own sailors to be ready. As elsewhere: *If any man will come after me, let him deny himself ((Matth. XVI))*, etc.

*And taking him. ((BEDA.))* With the affection of one that loves, saying: *Far be it from thee, Lord.* Or, as it is better had in the Greek: *Be thou merciful,* etc., *as far as* and he takes hold of him into his own affection, or leads him aside, lest he seem to rebuke his master while the rest are present.

*Go behind. ((ID.))* Many think that it was not Peter, but the adversary spirit, that was corrected, at whose suggestion the Apostle said this: But to me the Apostle's error, coming from the affection of piety, will never seem the devil's prompting. To the devil it is said: *Go behind, Satan.* To Peter: *Go behind me,* etc., that is, follow my judgment.

*The things that are of God,* etc. It is my will and the Father's that I should die for the salvation of men: thou wilt not have the grain of wheat fall into the ground, that it may bring forth much fruit.

*If any man will,* etc. ((BEDA.)) After he had shown the mystery of his passion and of his resurrection, he exhorts all to imitate the example of the passion, and to all he promises the salvation of souls. But to the more perfect he disclosed how great things he was to suffer, and that he was to rise again from the dead, giving thereby a form of preaching: namely, that each be instructed according to his own measure, and that higher things be not committed to the weak.

*Let him deny himself.* He is not able to lay hold of what is beyond himself, if he has not known how to slay what he is. Unless a man fail to his own self, he does not draw near to God, who is above him. *Let him take up his cross.* Either by wearing down the body through abstinence, or the mind through compassion. Of the body Paul says: *I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection ((II Cor. IX))*, etc. The same, of compassion of mind: *Who is weak, and I am not weak? ((II Cor. XI.))*

*For he that shall be ashamed. ((BEDA.))* The Church signifies two times: one of persecution, when the soul must be laid down; the other of peace, when earthly desires must be broken.

*For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc. Because many overcome avarice and despise things that pass away, but, hindered by bashfulness, do not utter with the voice the rightness of faith which they hold. He adds: *For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc.

notes.text: Given me — This and the following passages may be in some sort understood of the prophet Isaiah, but they are far more evidently and eminently verified in Christ, and indeed seem to be meant directly of him. The tongue - All ability of speaking plainly, and convincingly, and persuasively. Weary - Burdened with the sense of his, deplorable condition. Wakeneth - Me, from time to time, and continually. To hear - He by his Divine power assists me to the practice of all his commands and my duties, with all attention and diligence.
I gave — I patiently yielded up myself to those who smote me.

Justifieth — God will clear up my righteousness, and shew by many and mighty signs and wonders, that I lived and died his faithful servant. Let him come - l am conscious of mine own innocency, and I know that God will give sentence for me.
They — Mine accusers and enemies. The moth - Shall be cut off and consumed by a secret curse.

glossa.text: *The Lord hath given,* etc. ((ID.)) Although these things can be referred to Isaias, yet properly they are referred to Christ, as though he said: I who once wrought such things can now also work the like; my power is not diminished.

*As a garment.* ((ID.)) A garment is consumed by age and by the moth. The Jews too were called to penance for forty-two years after the Passion: at last, being negligent, they were crushed when the Romans came, and devoured by the moth of an evil conscience.

notes.text: The sorrows — Dangerous and deadly calamities. Pains - Such agonies and horrors, as dying persons use to feel.

Rest — Unto a chearful confidence in God. An exhortation to all nations to praise God for his mercy and truth, ver. 1, 2. The form of this psalm seems to be dramatical, and several parts of it are spoken in the name of several persons; as it is in the book of the Song of Solomon, and in one part of Ecclesiastes. David speaks in his own name from the beginning to ver. 22, from thence to ver. 25, in the name of the people; and thence to ver. 28, in the name of the priests; and then concludes in his own name. He calls upon all about him to praise God, ver. 1-4. Encourages himself and others to trust in God, from the experience he had had of his power and mercy, ver. 5-18. He gives thanks for his advancement to the throne, as it was a figure of the exaltation of Christ, ver. 19-23. The people, the priests, and the psalmist himself triumph in the prospect of the Redeemer's kingdom, ver. 24-29.

glossa.text:
*I have loved.* ((ID.)) This the sheep says which had strayed, the son returned, the pilgrim of this world.

((CASS.)) *I have loved.* Not for the temporal goods given to me, as the unbelievers do, but *because,* etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: *I will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him ((Psal. XLVIII))*. He is loved perfectly, him *eum*; read *cum*, "when" the mind is not moved by adverse things, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards expounds, *I have loved.* Not because he made me a king, or gave me prosperity, but because he hears my prayer in straits.

*And in my days.* ((AUG.)) Namely of my misery, which days I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labour and sorrow, that is, of the old rottenness.

*I will call upon.* Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? ((Rom. X.))* When therefore he says, *they shall call upon,* note that the lover is not idle. In which, *They have compassed me,* etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, in the time of fulness; whence: *Behold, now is the acceptable time,* etc. ((II Cor. VI)).

*Sorrows.* ((CASS.)) Sins, whence come the sorrow and the death of the soul; or eternal sorrows, and this shall be in hell. *The perils of hell.* ((AUG.)) For, steeped in carnal pleasure, I did not perceive the evils that compassed me about.
*Trouble and sorrow.* ((ID.)) As it were: those things first compassed me about, but afterwards I found trouble and sorrow, that is, outward affliction, to be profitable.

*O Lord, deliver.* ((CASS.)) Secondly he cries again, that being delivered he may come to rest. *The Lord is merciful.* ((AUG.)) Because he first inclined his ear to me and called me.

*Just.* Because he scourges again. *He hath mercy.* Because he receives unto blessedness. Nor ought that to be so bitter which he scourges, as that is sweet which he receives, because the Lord keeps the little ones, whom, when they are grown, he seeks for heirs.
*Turn thee.* ((ID.)) Not by thy merits or by thy strength, but because the Lord hath done well to thee.
*From death, the eyes.* ((ID.)) Death is unbelief; whence: *Let the dead bury their dead;* and again: *The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord ((Psal. CIII))*.
*I will please.* ((ID.)) He said, etc., *as far as* and this in the land of the living, who live eternally.

notes.text: Be not many teachers — Let no more of you take this upon you than God thrusts out; seeing it is so hard not to offend in speaking much. Knowing that we - That all who thrust themselves into the office. Shall receive greater condemnation - For more offenses. St. James here, as in several of the following verses, by a common figure of speech, includes himself: we shall receive, - we offend, - we put bits, - we curse - None of which, as common sense shows, are to be interpreted either of him or of the other apostles.
The same is able to bridle the whole body — That is, the whole man. And doubtless some are able to do this, and so are in this sense perfect.
We — That is, men.
Boasteth great things — Hath great influence.

A world of iniquity — Containing an immense quantity of all manner of wickedness. It defileth - As fire by its smoke. The whole body - The whole man. And setteth on fire the course of nature - All the passions, every wheel of his soul.
Every kind — The expression perhaps is not to be taken strictly. Reptiles - That is, creeping things.
But no man can tame the tongue — Of another; no, nor his own, without peculiar help from God.
Men made after the likeness of God — Indeed we have now lost this likeness; yet there remains from thence an indelible nobleness, which we ought to reverence both in ourselves and others.

glossa.text:
*Be ye not many masters.* As I have admonished you to do works, so I admonish you to shun foolish masterships. *Be ye not many.* There were many in the times of the apostles who, coming down from Judaea to Antioch, not well instructed in the law of the faith, taught that believers from among the Gentiles ought to be circumcised, and brought in other errors, which brought upon the true preachers no small labour of controversy. These therefore he removes from the office of the word, lest they hinder the true preachers.

*Greater. ((BED.))* He who, being unlearned, usurps the office of teaching, and announces Christ not sincerely, deserves a greater damnation than if he alone should perish by his own wickedness; as, on the contrary, he who ministers well acquires for himself a good degree.

*In many things.* Truly it is perilous to wish to be set over the rest, because not only you who are less instructed, but we all preachers, even the greater, offend in many things, some by teaching ill, and others by living ill, and in other ways. The blessed Apostle numbers himself with them, that he may reprove the more freely. The just man offends in one way, the wicked in another; the just man by the frailty of the flesh, and he does not cease to be just, whence Solomon: *Seven times in the day shall the just man fall and shall rise again;* as the offence is daily, so daily is the remedy of prayers and of good works, but the wicked fall down into evil. *If any man.* He wishes to show the unavoidable offence of the word, that he may deter the unskilled, lest they desire preferment: because he who desires to be set over others must be more perfect than the rest, lest he offend when he ought to profit; but the unskilled are not able not to offend in preaching.

*Offendeth not in word. ((BED.))* In that word, namely, whose offence human frailty is able to avoid. As the word of guile, of detraction, of pride, of boasting, and also of idle and superfluous speech, *he is a perfect man.*

*But if we put bits into the mouths of horses. ((BED.))* Into our own mouths much more ought we to put them. Certain books have: *But as bits to horses,* and it is thus joined to what follows: *But as we put bits into the mouths of horses, so the tongue also is indeed a little member, and exalteth great things.*

*And exalteth great things. ((ID.))* Rewards, if the impulse of him that directs governs it well; if ill, it exalts great destruction for itself and for its own, whence Solomon: *Death and life are in the hands of the tongue ((Prov. XVIII))* . It exalts life, if it teaches the Church well; death, if ill. For the matter is against those who, destitute both of life and of knowledge, presumed to teach. Great things therefore does that tongue exalt which, despising the words and the meanings of others, singularly boasts itself wise *sapientiem* and eloquent. Against which: *Do not multiply to speak lofty things, glorying.*

*Behold how great a fire.* So too an incontinent tongue makes a great matter of good works to perish, and so, since it is almost impossible that the sin of the tongue be avoided even by the perfect, not everyone ought to seek the mastership.

*The universality of iniquity.* He says universality, because through it almost all crimes are either contrived, as robberies, ravishments: or are perpetrated, as perjuries, false testimonies: or are defended, as when any impure man, by excusing the wickedness he has committed, feigns the good which he has not done. *Which defileth the whole body.* And because the tongue is such, it defiles the whole body, and makes it be reckoned unclean in the sight of God, and therefore it is a grave thing to undergo the mastership: because *it is set among our members,* it is one of our members, exceedingly near to us.

*It inflameth the wheel,* etc. ((BED.)) It defiles the whole course of temporal life, etc., *as far as* it compels to bring it to effect through the other members.

*For every nature of beasts,* etc. ((ID.)) We read in Pliny that a most savage asp in Egypt was tamed by a certain householder, and, going forth daily from its cavern, was wont to receive its allowance from his table. We read in Marcellinus that a tigress, made tame, was sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.

*Out of the same mouth proceedeth.* Others, seeing what we do, are led on by our example, so that they likewise bless and curse. *It ought not.* Truly it ought not to be that with the same mouth we bless concerning the head and curse concerning the members, because by the bitterness of cursing the sweetness of blessing is consumed.

*Doth a fountain.* The preacher must sometimes use bitter preaching, by withdrawing, by rebuking. Which is difficult enough, that with different words tending to the same end he should be able to do both.

*Can, brethren.* It cannot come to pass that a teacher be a fig tree by the sweetness of the beatitude to which he exhorts, and use sweet words, and that he be a vine, making men forget all temporal things, for which it behoves to use harsh ones: this therefore is difficult. *So neither can the salt water make sweet water,* that is, a preacher sharply biting the manners of others cannot in the same teaching be sweet to those same men.

notes.text: Matt. xvi, 13; Luke ix, 18.

He enjoined them silence for the present,

1. That he might not encourage the people to set him up for a temporal king;

2. That he might not provoke the scribes and Pharisees to destroy him before the time and,

3. That he might not forestall the bright evidence which was to be given of his Divine character after his resurrection.

31. Matt. xvi, 21; Luke ix, 22.
He spake that saying openly — Or in express terms. Till now he had only intimated it to them. And Peter taking hold of him - Perhaps by the arms or clothes.
Looking on his disciples — That they might the more observe what he said to Peter.

And when he called the people — To hear a truth of the last importance, and one that equally concerned them all. Let him deny himself - His own will, in all things small and great, however pleasing, and that continually: And take up his cross - Embrace the will of God, however painful, daily, hourly, continually. Thus only can he follow me in holiness to glory.
Matt. xvi, 25; Luke ix, 24; Luke xvii, 33; John xii, 25.

Whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words — That is, avowing whatever I have said (particularly of self denial and the daily cross) both by word and action. Matt. x, 32; Luke ix, 26; Luke xii, 8.

glossa.text:
*Whom do men say that I am?* Fitly does he first ask the opinion of men, lest their confession should seem weakened by the opinion of the crowd, but by the acknowledging of the truth: lest, like Herod, they be thought to waver about the things they had heard. Whence he says to Peter, according to Matthew: *Flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee ((Matth. XVI))*, that is, the teaching of men.

*Men.* Fitly are they called men who after the manner of men bring forth a divergent opinion concerning the Lord. For they who with a pious mind acknowledge the truth of his power deserve to be called, not men, but gods. Whence he says to them: *But you,* etc. As if he said: They, being men, opine the things of men; but you, being gods, whom do you say that I am?

*Thou art the Christ. ((BEDA.))* He embraces all things who expresses both the nature and the name, in which is the sum of the virtues. Paul says, etc., *as far as* yet it is not permitted to be ignorant of the faith of his generation.

*And he charged them. ((BEDA.))* He would not have himself preached before the passion and the resurrection: because, the sacrament of his blood being accomplished, he says to the apostles more opportunely: *Going, teach ye all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost ((Matth. XVIII))*. Because it would not profit that he be publicly preached whom they were about to see scourged, and crucified, and suffering many things.

*That it behoveth,* etc. ((HIER.)) As a skilled pilot, guarding against a storm while it is calm, wills his own sailors to be ready. As elsewhere: *If any man will come after me, let him deny himself ((Matth. XVI))*, etc.

*And taking him. ((BEDA.))* With the affection of one that loves, saying: *Far be it from thee, Lord.* Or, as it is better had in the Greek: *Be thou merciful,* etc., *as far as* and he takes hold of him into his own affection, or leads him aside, lest he seem to rebuke his master while the rest are present.

*Go behind. ((ID.))* Many think that it was not Peter, but the adversary spirit, that was corrected, at whose suggestion the Apostle said this: But to me the Apostle's error, coming from the affection of piety, will never seem the devil's prompting. To the devil it is said: *Go behind, Satan.* To Peter: *Go behind me,* etc., that is, follow my judgment.

*The things that are of God,* etc. It is my will and the Father's that I should die for the salvation of men: thou wilt not have the grain of wheat fall into the ground, that it may bring forth much fruit.

*If any man will,* etc. ((BEDA.)) After he had shown the mystery of his passion and of his resurrection, he exhorts all to imitate the example of the passion, and to all he promises the salvation of souls. But to the more perfect he disclosed how great things he was to suffer, and that he was to rise again from the dead, giving thereby a form of preaching: namely, that each be instructed according to his own measure, and that higher things be not committed to the weak.

*Let him deny himself.* He is not able to lay hold of what is beyond himself, if he has not known how to slay what he is. Unless a man fail to his own self, he does not draw near to God, who is above him. *Let him take up his cross.* Either by wearing down the body through abstinence, or the mind through compassion. Of the body Paul says: *I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection ((II Cor. IX))*, etc. The same, of compassion of mind: *Who is weak, and I am not weak? ((II Cor. XI.))*

*For he that shall be ashamed. ((BEDA.))* The Church signifies two times: one of persecution, when the soul must be laid down; the other of peace, when earthly desires must be broken.

*For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc. Because many overcome avarice and despise things that pass away, but, hindered by bashfulness, do not utter with the voice the rightness of faith which they hold. He adds: *For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The Teacher turns and asks the old question.
Who do you say that I am?
Not a rumor, not a guess —
You are the Messiah, the Christ of God.
Then take up your cross and come.
We will lose our lives to find them.
Come, let us worship the Lord who walks ahead.
We come to follow Jesus. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: On the road to Caesarea Jesus stops and turns: Who do people say that I am? And then, closer: Who do you say that I am?
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
He sets his face toward the city like flint, like the servant who would not turn away though they struck him.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
He says the hard thing plainly: take up the cross, lose your life, and you will find it again.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
So we lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord. Come, let us worship.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Jesus turns and asks who we say he is.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
He sets his face toward the cross.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
He calls us to lose our lives and find them.
You are the Messiah; we will follow you.
Come, let us worship and walk behind him.
We come to follow Jesus. Amen.
